title: Money Bank Call Center
author: Guruprasad Sankaranarayanan (Kellogg 2012); edited by Nikola Jakić (Kellogg 2016), Elizabeth Henry (Kellogg 2020)
industry_source_label: X06 Financial Services; X10 Legal & Professional Services
fit_question: If you were a partner and could choose to work on any type of case, what would you do? What do you think you would learn?
prompt: Our client is a large financial services firm with multiple locations around the world. Part of their service offering includes a 24-hour helpline. The client has their call centers in New York and Paris. The client has recently acquired a small firm (Firm B) in order to expand its reach in a particular geography. Firm B provides a subset of the services and has its call center located in the Philippines. The client has asked us to determine its strategy going forward for handling customer calls. In particular they want us to look into the call center operations.

clarifying_info.answer: Provides full range of financial services for individuals and small organizations. Acquired firm (Firm B) was started 5 years ago and is still run by the original founders.
New employees are college graduates with basic knowledge of financial services and products. Fluency in English and several European languages is required.
Very difficult to lay off employees in the Paris location & significant costs will be incurred. Philippines government encourages investment in the country & significant tax advantage possible.
All three call centers are currently operating at capacity; there is no slack at any location.
Currently, there is space and infrastructure necessary to expand the Philippines facility. Assume overhead is variable in this case.

interviewer_notes: This is an outsourcing case with the following elements: use a framework that covers the most important areas of M&A and cost cutting; read the exhibits to assess the cost effectiveness and efficiency of the 3 locations; discuss qualitative information on the acquired company (products, culture, customers, etc.). There is no right or wrong recommendation, as it depends on the interviewee's assessment of the qualitative concerns. Key case steps: (1) evaluate existing and potential cost structure, (2) explore alternative ideas for implementation, (3) provide client recommendation.

suggested_framework.summary: A cost/operations framework crossed with M&A-integration considerations for the acquired call center.

children.label: Current utilization / slack at each center
Nature and culture of acquired firm (Firm B)

stages.interviewer_asks: Reads the case prompt and asks the candidate to lay out how they would approach the problem.
stages.expected_answer: A framework covering the cost structure of the three call centers (employee cost, overhead, efficiency), integration/capacity considerations from the acquisition, and qualitative/regulatory risk factors, oriented toward a cost-reduction and M&A-integration decision.
good_answer_signals: Separates quantitative cost/efficiency analysis from qualitative M&A integration issues
Mentions regulatory/labor law differences across geographies

stages.interviewer_asks: Candidate asks clarifying questions about the client, the call centers, and the regulatory environment.
stages.info_to_release: Client characteristics, call center staffing/language requirements, and regulatory environment in NY/Paris/Philippines (see clarifying_info).
stages.expected_answer: Candidate should surface that Paris layoffs are costly/difficult and that the Philippines offers tax incentives, since these will matter for the recommendation.

stages.interviewer_asks: Part 1: Evaluate existing and potential cost structure. Provide Exhibit A when the candidate asks about call center performance.
stages.release_when: When candidate asks about call center performance/cost data
stages.info_to_release: Exhibit A (calls/year, employee cost/year, overhead cost/year, # employees by center); total combined cost of the 3 firms is $9.6M; Philippines currently processes calls at half the efficiency of NY per employee; all centers operate at capacity.
stages.expected_answer: Candidate computes calls/employee for each center (NY 8,000; Paris 6,667; Philippines 4,000), recognizes Philippines is least efficient, and calculates that moving all volume to the Philippines requires 250 additional employees (325 total, up from 75), producing new operating cost of $7.8M and net annual savings of $1.8M versus the $9.6M status quo. Candidate should then probe further and learn there is also a one-time cost of $5M (severance for NY/Paris, facility expansion), which the interviewer should reveal once cost savings alone have been identified.
good_answer_signals: Arrives at $7.8M new cost / $1.8M net savings
Asks whether there are any one-time/transition costs

stages.interviewer_asks: Part 2: The client will not budge on a two-year breakeven requirement. Prompt the candidate to explore ways to make outsourcing to the Philippines feasible.
stages.info_to_release: Options: decrease the $5M investment cost, or increase the efficiency of Philippines employees (guide interviewee toward the latter). If asked, best practices can be transferred and implemented within 3-6 months; overheads are assumed to double with the need for better equipment if efficiency is raised.
stages.expected_answer: Candidate should first note that $1.8M/year savings against a $5M one-time cost implies roughly a 2.8-year payback, which misses the 2-year target. Candidate should then explore raising Philippines efficiency to NY's level (8,000 calls/employee/year): ~162.5 employees needed (round to 160), new employee cost $3.2M, new overhead $2.6M (double the $1.3M base), new total cost $5.8M — $3.8M savings vs. status quo and $2M better than the un-improved outsourcing option. Candidate should also raise talent-availability, customer-satisfaction, legal/layoff-timing, and public-opinion questions.
good_answer_signals: Recognizes the base plan misses the 2-year breakeven
Correctly recalculates cost at improved efficiency ($5.8M total)
Raises talent, customer satisfaction, legal, and PR risk questions unprompted

stages.interviewer_asks: What other qualitative or risk considerations should factor into the recommendation?
stages.expected_answer: Risks of increasing Philippines capacity by 200%+ (people, infrastructure, service quality, knowledge-transfer gaps, organizational change); reputational impact and whether customers notice service differences or competitors exploit the change; nature/culture of the acquired firm and the markets it serves.

stages.interviewer_asks: Part 3: Provide your recommendation to the client.
stages.expected_answer: This is open-ended; a strong answer includes: (1) Recommendation — e.g., outsource to Philippines with an efficiency-improvement plan, explicitly weighing the risks of outsourcing against the acquired firm's nature; (2) Risks — capacity scale-up risk, reputational/competitive risk; (3) Next steps — assess infrastructure requirements and capabilities, recruit the right talent, ensure smooth transfer and implementation of best practices. Excellent candidates proactively raise the efficiency-improvement lever and address the qualitative context (nature of the merger, markets served) without being prompted.
good_answer_signals: States a clear recommendation with rationale

exhibits.title: Exhibit A – Call Center Performance FY 2010
exhibits.description: Table of the three call centers (New York, Paris, Philippines) showing calls/year, employee cost/year, overhead cost/year, and number of employees.
exhibits.key_insight: Philippines has the lowest calls-per-employee (4,000) versus New York (8,000) and Paris (6,667), despite the lowest per-employee cost — it is currently the least efficient center even though it is the cheapest per head.

math.question: How many additional employees does the Philippines call center need to handle all 1.3M annual calls at its current efficiency, and what is the resulting net annual savings?
givens: Philippines current efficiency = 300,000 calls / 75 employees = 4,000 calls/employee/year
Current combined operating cost of the 3 centers = $9.6M
Philippines employee cost = $20,000/employee/year; overhead is variable, $300,000 OH / 300,000 calls = $1/call
steps: Employees needed = 1,300,000 calls / 4,000 calls per employee = 325 employees
math.answer: 250 additional employees needed; new operating cost $7.8M; net annual savings of $1.8M versus the $9.6M status quo

math.question: Given a one-time transition cost of $5M and the client's 2-year breakeven requirement, does the base outsourcing plan (Philippines at current efficiency) meet the target?
givens: One-time cost = $5M (severance for NY/Paris, Philippines facility expansion)
Net annual savings from the base plan (m1) = $1.8M/year
steps: 2.8 years exceeds the client's required 2-year breakeven
math.answer: Approximately 2.8 years — the base plan fails the 2-year breakeven requirement, so it is not profitable enough to pursue as-is

math.question: If Philippines call-center efficiency is raised to match New York (8,000 calls/employee/year), what is the new total operating cost and savings?
givens: Target efficiency = 8,000 calls/employee/year (same as New York)
Overhead is assumed to double versus the $1.3M base-plan overhead (better equipment needed)
Status quo cost = $9.6M; base outsourcing plan cost (m1) = $7.8M
math.answer: New total operating cost $5.8M; $3.8M savings vs. status quo and $2.0M better than the un-improved outsourcing plan

synthesis: Open-ended: a strong recommendation states a clear direction (e.g., outsource to the Philippines paired with an efficiency-improvement program to hit the 2-year breakeven), explicitly weighs the risks of scaling capacity 200%+ and reputational/competitive exposure against the acquired firm's nature and markets, and lays out next steps (assess infrastructure needs, recruit talent, manage best-practice transfer).
what_great_looks_like: Proactively identifies raising Philippines efficiency as the lever to hit the 2-year breakeven, without being prompted
Integrates the qualitative M&A context (nature of Firm B, markets served, regulatory differences) into the final recommendation, not just the cost math
Structures the recommendation as recommendation / risks / next steps
common_pitfalls: Stopping at the $1.8M net-savings figure without probing for one-time transition costs
Missing that overhead is variable per call, and mis-scaling overhead when volume or efficiency changes
Giving a recommendation without addressing regulatory/layoff constraints in Paris or reputational risk

extraction.notes: Book's own figures ($7.8M, $1.8M, $3.2M, $2.6M, $5.8M, $3.8M, $2M) were independently recomputed and matched exactly.
